title: Risk & issue management in linear vs iterative projects
blurb: Explain why risk and issue stages run differently in linear and iterative life cycles, with the strengths and weaknesses of each.
question: A city council is replacing its parking permit service: new roadside signs and meters delivered in a linear way, and a resident app built iteratively. How should risk identification, monitoring and escalation, and the handling of issues, differ between the two parts, and what are the pros and cons of each approach?

teach.body: Both life cycles use the same risk stages (identification, analysis, monitoring, escalation, response, closure) and the same issue stages (logging and analysis, escalation, assignment of actions). What differs is WHEN they happen, HOW OFTEN, HOW FORMALLY, WHO owns them and WHERE escalation goes. The reason is the life cycle itself: linear commits to a defined scope early, while iterative lets requirements emerge in short, fixed time boxes.

teach.h: Risk and issue management side by side

rows.label: Identification
values: Up front, then at each gate

teach.h: Linear: risk work anchored to phases and gates

items.label: Early risks shape the business case and options
Full identification; register and contingency set
Formal risk review before committing further
Remaining risks closed or handed over to BAU

teach.caption: Big commitments are made early in linear projects, so risks must be understood before each gate is passed.

teach.h: Iterative: risk spotted in every time box
teach.caption: Planning: risks in the chosen items. Stand-up: blockers and new risks. Review: wrong assumptions exposed. Retrospective: improve how risk is handled.

teach.body: In a LINEAR project, scope is fixed early and late change is costly, so the team must find risks before committing: thorough up-front identification, a formal register and governance at gates give the sponsor assurance. In an ITERATIVE project, requirements emerge and each time box delivers something users can test. That SHORT FEEDBACK LOOP reduces exposure: the biggest risk, building the wrong thing, is checked every few weeks. Risky items are often tackled early by prioritising them in the backlog.

teach.h: Issues: formal route versus fast fix
teach.body: LINEAR: issues are logged in the issue log, analysed for impact, escalated to the sponsor if beyond tolerance, and actions assigned, often through formal change control because the scope is baselined. ITERATIVE: blockers surface at the daily stand-up and the team clears most of them within the time box. If resolving one changes scope, the product owner reprioritises the backlog. Issues that threaten the fixed time, cost or overall objectives are escalated to the product owner or sponsor.

head: Approach
Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: Whole-project view early; feeds business case and contingency; clear audit trail
Emerging risks found late; register can go stale; heavier paperwork
Risks found as they emerge; fast feedback; team owns and acts quickly
Long-term, cross-cutting risks can be missed; less formal record; relies on team discipline

teach.body: The signs and meters are a physical build with fixed requirements, so they follow a linear life cycle: a Definition-stage workshop finds risks such as late meter delivery, the register is baselined with contingency, and risks are reviewed at each gate and escalated through the board. The resident app is iterative: payment-provider risks are raised in time-box planning, a login blocker is cleared after a stand-up, and a risky integration is pulled to the top of the backlog. The sponsor sees one combined risk report.

teach.text: Two exam traps. Iterative does NOT mean 'no risk register' or 'no escalation': risks are still recorded and escalated to the product owner or sponsor. And linear does NOT mean 'identify risks once at the start': risks are revisited at every gate and through periodic reviews.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State the stage being compared (often identification) and that both life cycles still use it.
Linear: up front and at gates, formal register, periodic reviews, escalation via governance.
Iterative: continuous each iteration (planning, stand-ups, retrospectives), team ownership, backlog.
Give an advantage and a disadvantage of each (e.g. early whole view vs late discovery).
Relate it to the scenario: fixed physical build versus evolving software.
Same risk and issue stages in both; timing, frequency, formality, ownership and escalation differ.
Linear: identify up front and at gates; formal register; periodic reviews; escalate via governance.
Iterative: identify continuously; team ownership; risks shape backlog priority; short feedback loops cut exposure.
Issues: linear often via formal change control; iterative often via stand-ups and backlog reprioritising.
Linear can find emerging risks late; iterative can miss long-term, cross-cutting risks.

summary: You can now explain how and why risk and issue management differ between linear and iterative life cycles, stage by stage. You can also weigh the strengths and weaknesses of each approach, which is exactly what a 5-mark written answer on this topic asks for.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, when is risk identification mainly carried out?
options: Only once, at the very first workshop
Up front, then revisited at each gate
Only after deployment work has begun
Only when an issue has already occurred
A.why: Linear projects identify risks thoroughly up front and revisit them at each decision gate and in periodic reviews.

whyNot.0: Risks are revisited throughout; one workshop would leave the register stale.
whyNot.2: Waiting until deployment is too late to shape the business case and plans.
whyNot.3: Risk identification is proactive; an issue has already happened.

A.q: In an iterative project, where are new risks and blockers most commonly raised day to day?
options: Gate reviews
Daily stand-ups
Annual audits
Closure reports
A.why: Iterative teams surface blockers and new risks at the daily stand-up, as well as in time-box planning and retrospectives.

whyNot.0: Gate reviews belong to linear life cycles and are not daily.
whyNot.2: Audits are occasional assurance activities, not day-to-day risk identification.
whyNot.3: Closure reports come at the end, far too late for day-to-day risks.

A.q: In iterative delivery, how are significant risks often reflected in planning?
options: They shape the priority of backlog items
They are held back until the final release
They are only recorded at the post-project review
They are passed straight to the portfolio board
A.why: Risks are reflected in the backlog: risky items may be tackled early so problems surface while there's time to react.

whyNot.1: Deferring risky work to the end increases exposure.
whyNot.2: Waiting for the post-project review means no action during delivery.
whyNot.3: Most risks are owned and managed by the team; only those beyond limits are escalated.

B.q: Why do the short feedback loops of an iterative life cycle reduce risk exposure?
options: Risks no longer need to be recorded
The sponsor no longer needs to approve
Time boxes remove all technical risk
Wrong assumptions surface within weeks
B.why: Users test each increment, so misunderstandings and technical problems show up quickly, while they are still cheap to fix.

whyNot.0: Risks are still recorded, in a register and reflected in the backlog.
whyNot.1: Governance still applies; the sponsor still takes escalated decisions.
whyNot.2: Time boxes don't remove risk; they expose it sooner.

B.q: In a linear construction project, a risk now exceeds the project manager's tolerance. How is it most likely escalated?
options: Via a team retrospective
Via backlog refinement
Via the formal route to the sponsor
Via an informal word with the end users
B.why: Linear projects escalate through formal governance: the PM raises the risk to the sponsor or board.

whyNot.0: Retrospectives are an iterative improvement ceremony, not an escalation route.
whyNot.1: Backlog refinement is an iterative practice led by the product owner.
whyNot.3: Users lack the authority to decide on risks beyond the PM's tolerance.

B.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of identifying risks mainly up front in a linear project?
options: There is no formal record for assurance
Emerging risks may only be found late
Contingency cannot be estimated at all
The business case lacks any risk data
B.why: Risks that emerge during delivery may not be spotted until the next gate or review, when they are costlier to handle.

whyNot.0: A formal record is a strength of the linear approach.
whyNot.2: Up-front identification is what allows contingency to be estimated.
whyNot.3: Early risk work feeds the business case: a strength, not a weakness.

C.q: A housing association is building a new block of flats (linear) and a tenant repairs app (iterative), under one sponsor. Which approach to risk identification is most appropriate?
options: One workshop at the start for both parts
Gate reviews for both; no stand-ups at all
Per-iteration checks for both, no register
Gate-based for flats, each iteration for app
C.why: Each part should use the rhythm of its life cycle: up front and at gates for the build, continuously each iteration for the app.

whyNot.0: A single workshop leaves both registers stale as work progresses.
whyNot.1: Gates alone would miss the app's emerging risks between reviews.
whyNot.2: The physical build needs a formal register and gate reviews; iterative risks still need recording too.

C.q: Midway through a two-week time box, a developer finds the shared test environment is down, blocking their work. Under a typical iterative approach, what should happen first?
options: Raise it at stand-up so it's cleared fast
Submit a formal change request to the board
Wait for the next gate review to log it
Add it to the post-project lessons log
C.why: Blockers are raised at the daily stand-up and the team acts quickly to clear them within the time box; escalation follows only if it threatens time, cost or objectives.

whyNot.1: No baselined scope is changing; a formal change request would be slow and unnecessary.
whyNot.2: Iterative projects don't wait for gates; the time box would be lost.
whyNot.3: Lessons can be captured later, but the blocker needs action now.

C.q: Which THREE describe risk management in an iterative life cycle? 1. Risks identified continuously each iteration. 2. Team-level ownership of risks. 3. A register baselined at Definition and reviewed only at gates. 4. Risks reflected in backlog priorities.
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
C.why: Iterative risk management is continuous (1), owned at team level (2) and built into backlog priorities (4).

whyNot.1: Statement 3 describes a linear approach, and 2 is a genuine iterative feature.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 describes a linear approach, and 1 is a genuine iterative feature.

reteach.title: Think of building a house versus running a pop-up restaurant
reteach.question: A builder constructs a house to an approved design; a chef runs a pop-up that changes its menu each week based on diners' feedback. How does each one handle what might go wrong?

blocks.h: Plan it all first, or learn as you go
blocks.body: The builder must think hard about risks BEFORE pouring foundations: ground conditions, planning approval, material delays. Once the concrete is down, changes are expensive, so the builder checks risks again at each stage sign-off. The chef tries new dishes every week. If diners hate the risotto, it's off the menu next week: the risk of a bad dish is small because feedback is fast. The chef's team spots problems every service and fixes them on the spot.

blocks.text: The chef still needs to think ahead about big risks, like the venue's lease ending. Iterative teams must keep an eye on long-term risks, not just this week's.

explain.body: Risks identified thoroughly up front, recorded in a formal register, reviewed periodically and at every decision gate, and escalated through formal governance to the sponsor or board.

test.q: What role do decision gates play in risk management on a linear project?
options: They replace the need for a register
They hand all risks to the supplier
They review risks before committing
They are used only to close issues
test.why: Each gate is a formal point to review the risk position before the sponsor commits further time and money.

whyNot.0: The register is still kept; gates use it.
whyNot.1: Gates don't transfer risks to suppliers.
whyNot.3: Gates review the whole position, including live risks, not just issues.

explain.body: Risks identified continuously at time-box planning, daily stand-ups and retrospectives. The team owns most risks, risky items are prioritised in the backlog, and escalation goes to the product owner or sponsor.

test.q: Who usually owns day-to-day risks in an iterative project?
options: The portfolio board
The delivery team
An external auditor
The finance team
test.why: Iterative risk management relies on team-level ownership, with the team spotting and acting on risks every iteration.

whyNot.0: The portfolio board deals with strategic, cross-project decisions.
whyNot.2: Auditors provide assurance; they don't own delivery risks.
whyNot.3: Finance supports budgeting but doesn't own delivery risks.

explain.body: Linear: issue log, impact analysis, escalation beyond tolerance to the sponsor, actions often via formal change control. Iterative: blockers raised at stand-up and cleared fast; scope effects handled by backlog reprioritising; bigger issues to the product owner or sponsor.

explain.h: Iterative issue: where does it go?

test.q: On an iterative project, resolving a problem means swapping a planned feature for a more urgent fix. How is this usually handled?
options: A formal change request to the project board
The sponsor rewrites the business case
The release date is moved back a month
The product owner reprioritises the backlog
test.why: Within the fixed time and cost, scope changes are absorbed by the product owner reprioritising the backlog.

whyNot.0: Formal change control is reserved for changes to fixed time, cost or overall objectives.
whyNot.1: A feature swap within the time box doesn't change the project's justification.
whyNot.2: Iterative delivery fixes the date and flexes scope.

explain.body: Linear gives an early, whole-project view and a strong audit trail but may find emerging risks late. Iterative catches risks as they emerge but can miss long-term, cross-cutting risks and keeps a lighter record.

test.q: Which is a typical weakness of risk management in an iterative life cycle?
options: Long-term, cross-cutting risks can be missed
Feedback arrives too slowly to be useful
Risks are only identified at the very start
Team members are not allowed to raise risks
test.why: With attention on each time box, risks spanning the whole project or other projects can be overlooked unless someone looks at the bigger picture.

whyNot.1: Fast feedback is a strength of iterative delivery.
whyNot.2: That describes a poorly run linear approach, not iterative.
whyNot.3: Team members raising risks is central to the iterative approach.
